screens.title: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what an InnoDB Cluster is and why it simplifies high availability for MySQL. InnoDB Cluster is not a separate database engine. It is a packaged solution that binds three components together: Group Replication for consistent multi-primary safety and failover, MySQL Shell as the control plane with dba utilities for provisioning, and MySQL Router to present a stable connection endpoint to applications. Together they reduce manual configuration, automate failover, and hide topology changes from client code. You will see concrete commands used to prepare instances and bootstrap a cluster, understand how Router maps write traffic to the current primary and read traffic to secondaries, and learn common pitfalls such as missing GTID configuration or incorrect server identifiers. A short workflow will guide you from preparing instances to bootstrapping the cluster and deploying Router so your application can continue without code changes when failover happens. By the end you should be able to explain the role of each component, run the key dba functions in MySQL Shell, and reason about how Router keeps application connections stable. What operational change would you prioritize first to keep an application highly available?

Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › Overview
Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster
Provision, operate, and route client traffic for a robust MySQL HA solution.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
This module teaches the operational workflow: prepare instances with MySQL Shell's dba utilities, bootstrap a Group Replication cluster with dba.createCluster, add and remove members safely, and configure MySQL Router for transparent client routing and automatic failover. Along the way we call out common pitfalls and the configuration checks that dba.configureInstance performs.
Group Replication
Consistency & failover
MySQL Shell
Provisioning & management
MySQL Router
Transparent client routing
Explore Key Topics
Provisioning
dba.configureInstance automates checks and config to avoid manual errors.
Bootstrap
dba.createCluster bootstraps Group Replication and elects a primary.
Routing
MySQL Router maps writes to primary and reads to secondaries, enabling failover without app changes.
Concept Map
Group Replication
Provides the group protocol, replication, and automated failover that the cluster uses to keep data consistent.
MySQL Shell
Acts as the control plane with dba utilities that automate configuration, bootstrap, and membership operations.
MySQL Router
Provides an application-facing endpoint that routes writes to the PRIMARY and reads to SECONDARY nodes, and adapts automatically after failover.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over these next screens you will develop a set of practical skills to manage an InnoDB Cluster. First, you will learn how MySQL Shell and MySQL Router integrate with Group Replication so the whole stack forms one operational unit. This matters because managing raw Group Replication without a control plane and routing layer leaves you handling many low-level configuration steps manually. Second, you will practice using MySQL Shell's dba utilities to prepare instances, bootstrap a cluster, and view cluster health. These utilities automate configuration checks and user creation to reduce human error, and you will see exact commands used in examples. Third and fourth objectives are procedural: you will configure MySQL Router so client connections are routed transparently to the correct node, and you will perform common administrative tasks such as adding or removing instances using the cluster object. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone so you can check your progress and repeat steps safely. Think of these skills as operational habits: prepare carefully, bootstrap intentionally, and rely on Router so applications don't need custom failover logic.

screens.title: What is MySQL InnoDB Cluster?
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: an InnoDB Cluster is an operational bundle that uses Group Replication, MySQL Shell, and MySQL Router to deliver a complete high-availability solution for MySQL. That means the cluster is not a single new product, but rather a curated integration. Group Replication provides the group protocol and automated failover. MySQL Shell provides the dba utilities that perform the heavy lifting of configuration, user creation, and membership orchestration. MySQL Router acts as the lightweight proxy that keeps application connection strings stable while it routes writes to the primary and reads to secondaries. A concrete example helps. Imagine a three-node deployment where one node is primary and two are secondaries. If the primary fails, Group Replication elects a new primary. MySQL Router, which has been bootstrapped against the cluster, detects this and starts routing write traffic to the new primary without changes to the application. A common misconception is thinking InnoDB Cluster replaces manual replication configuration; it actually automates and orchestrates those steps. The practical takeaway is operational: use Shell to configure and maintain members, rely on Router for transparent client access, and view Group Replication as the protocol that enforces consistency. How does that change your checklist for deploying a production MySQL cluster?

keyIdea.text: InnoDB Cluster = Group Replication + MySQL Shell + MySQL Router, packaged to automate HA deployment and routing.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › What is InnoDB Cluster?
Definition
InnoDB Cluster ties together the core replication protocol, an automation toolset, and a routing layer to deliver a manageable HA architecture. This reduces manual configuration steps and centralizes cluster operations.
Group Replication
Consistency, membership, and automated failover.
MySQL Shell
dba utilities for provisioning, bootstrap, and management.
MySQL Router
Transparent client routing and automatic failover handling.
Key Takeaway

Think of InnoDB Cluster as an operational pattern that packages replication, automation, and routing so that failover and client connectivity are easier to operate safely.

Concrete Example
A three-node cluster where writes must always reach the primary and reads can be served by secondaries. When the primary fails, Group Replication elects a new primary. Router detects the change and redirects writes automatically so the application experiences minimal disruption.
Common misconception
People sometimes think InnoDB Cluster removes the need for correct instance configuration. It doesn't. Proper GTID, unique server_id, and network reachability are still required; Shell helps enforce these checks.
Why it matters
Reduces manual setup, lowers human error, and provides a single operational model for HA.
Try this
Plan a checklist for each node: GTID on, unique server_id, reachable network, and admin account for MySQL Shell.

screens.title: MySQL Shell dba utilities
screens.narratorSegment: MySQL Shell acts as the control plane with a small set of dba utilities that make configuring an InnoDB Cluster straightforward. The important functions you will use are dba. configureInstance, dba. createCluster, cluster. addInstance, cluster. removeInstance, and cluster. status. Each performs multi-step actions: configure applies recommended server variables and creates internal users, createCluster bootstraps Group Replication and chooses the initial primary, addInstance handles state transfer and membership, and status summarizes health and topology. A concrete demonstration is helpful: you would connect to a member with MySQL Shell and run dba. configureInstance for each node. After preparing nodes, running dba. createCluster on one node bootstraps the group and exposes the cluster object. Then use cluster. addInstance to bring secondaries online. A common misconception is that these utilities are only wrappers for S Q L commands; instead, they implement validation, automated user setup, and guided workflows that reduce manual mistakes. When you practice, verify that the MySQL Shell user has administrative privileges and that network connectivity between nodes and the shell is open. Try this mentally: prepare all nodes, bootstrap once, then add members. What validation step would block a misconfigured node from joining?

keyIdea.title: dba utilities
keyIdea.text: dba utilities automate checks and multi-step configuration so provisioning and membership changes are safe and repeatable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › dba utilities
Core dba commands
These commands perform validation and automation steps so you don't run individual SQL statements on each server. They create users, set required variables, and orchestrate group membership.
mysqlsh root@192.168.1.10:3306 --sql

# Prepare an instance
# dba.configureInstance('user@host:port')
dba.configureInstance('root@192.168.1.10:3306')

# Bootstrap a cluster
# dba.createCluster('mycluster')
dba.createCluster('mycluster')

# Add a prepared instance
# cluster.addInstance('user@host:port')
cluster.addInstance('root@192.168.1.11:3306')

# Check status
cluster.status()
Explanation & example
  • dba.configureInstance: validates prerequisites, sets GTID and replication variables, and creates required accounts.
  • dba.createCluster: bootstraps Group Replication using the prepared instance as the initial primary.
  • cluster.addInstance: performs state transfer and joins the instance to the group safely.
  • cluster.status: returns topology, roles, and status so you can confirm the cluster health.
Common mistake
Attempting to add an unprepared instance is a frequent error. dba.configureInstance prevents this by checking GTID, server_id, and required privileges before the join.

screens.title: Preparing instances with dba.configureInstance()
screens.narratorSegment: Preparing an instance is an essential first step. dba. configureInstance runs a set of prerequisite checks and applies recommended configurations automatically. It verifies GTID mode and related variables, ensures server_id is unique, checks that binary logging is enabled, and validates network reachability. It also creates internal accounts and privileges required for Group Replication to operate. In practice you will run this on every instance you plan to join to the cluster. For example, running dba. configureInstance for root at 192.168.1.11 will check GTID, apply variables, and create the replication user if missing. The practical significance is that this single command replaces several manual steps that are easy to forget. A common misconception is that dba. configureInstance will silently override all settings; in reality it performs guided changes and reports warnings when it cannot apply a change. If a node fails the checks, address the specific issue—enable GTID or fix server_id—before attempting to add it to the cluster. A simple mental workflow: run configureInstance, fix reported issues, then proceed to bootstrap or add that node. Which prerequisite do you check first on a fresh instance?

keyIdea.title: Prepare before you join
keyIdea.text: Use dba.configureInstance to validate GTID, server_id, binary logging, network, and privileges so nodes can join safely.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › Preparing instances
Preparation steps
1. Check GTID and binary logging
GTID must be enabled for Group Replication to work smoothly and for state transfer to function.
2. Ensure unique server_id
Duplicate identifiers break membership assumptions; dba.configureInstance verifies uniqueness.
3. Validate network reachability and ports
Nodes and the Shell must communicate over the appropriate network ports for safe joins and routing discovery.
4. Create required users
The function can create internal accounts needed for group replication and for Shell operations.
Example
-- In MySQL Shell, connected to a node
# Prepare a node for cluster membership
# dba.configureInstance('root@192.168.1.11:3306')

# Shell output will list checks and applied changes or warnings
# Fix any reported issues and re-run before joining
Pitfall
Skipping configuration means state transfer or join may fail later. Always resolve configureInstance warnings before proceeding.

screens.title: Bootstrapping a cluster with dba.createCluster()
screens.narratorSegment: Bootstrapping a cluster is the moment a group is formed. When you run dba. createCluster on a prepared instance, MySQL Shell configures Group Replication on that node and initializes the group. That instance becomes the initial primary and the replication group is established. The Shell returns a cluster object which you use for subsequent management. It is important to bootstrap only from a prepared instance, and only once per cluster. Trying to bootstrap a second time against a different prepared node creates conflicting groups. As a concrete example, after preparing three nodes, run dba. createCluster('MyCluster') on one node. The Shell sets the necessary group replication variables, creates the underlying group, and exposes management methods through the returned object. A common misconception is that bootstrapping will automatically add other prepared nodes; instead, you must call cluster. addInstance for each additional member. After bootstrapping, verify readiness with cluster. status. Operationally, plan to bootstrap during a maintenance window and ensure Router is configured after the cluster is stable. What checks would you perform before bootstrapping in production? Bootstrapping a cluster with dba.createCluster() means run dba.createcluster on one prepared instance to initialize group replication; then add other members with cluster.addinstance.. In practical terms, how a cluster is initialized and what becomes the primary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › Bootstrapping
Bootstrap steps
Select one prepared instance and run dba.createCluster. This sets group variables and makes that instance the primary. The command returns a cluster object for management.
# Example in MySQL Shell
# Assuming node prepared
dba.createCluster('MyCluster')

# Shell returns a cluster object used for management:
# mycluster = dba.getCluster('MyCluster')
# Then add other nodes with mycluster.addInstance(...)
Notes & checks
  • Bootstrap only one time per cluster; do not run createCluster from multiple nodes.
  • After bootstrapping, use the cluster object to add members and manage health.
  • Common mistake: assuming other prepared nodes join automatically; explicit addInstance calls are required.
Key Takeaway

Bootstrap once from a validated instance, then add others. Validate cluster.status immediately after bootstrapping to confirm topology.

screens.title: MySQL Router: transparent client routing
screens.narratorSegment: MySQL Router is the lightweight middleware that sits between your application and the InnoDB Cluster. Its job is simple but crucial: provide transparent routing so application connection strings do not need to change when a primary failover occurs. When Router boots against a cluster, it discovers topology information from Shell and maintains an internal view of primary and secondary instances. It directs write connections to the primary and can load-balance read connections across secondaries. For example, a common bootstrap command is mysqlrouter --bootstrap user@host:port --cluster-type=gr which connects to a cluster member and writes a local Router configuration that points to the cluster. A practical scenario: your application uses Router's endpoint for both reads and writes. If the primary fails and Group Replication elects a new primary, Router detects the change and starts routing writes to the new primary without requiring application-side reconnection logic. A common misconception is that Router performs complex transaction routing; it does not change query semantics. Its role is connection routing and load distribution. For operational safety, ensure Router's listening ports are reachable by application servers and that the bootstrap account used has appropriate privileges to query cluster topology. How would you validate Router after bootstrapping?

keyIdea.title: Router role
keyIdea.text: MySQL Router provides a stable application endpoint that routes writes to the primary and reads to secondaries, and adapts automatically after failover.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › MySQL Router
Responsibilities
  • Provide a stable connection endpoint for applications.
  • Route write (read-write) traffic to the current primary.
  • Load-balance read-only traffic across secondaries.
  • Automatically adapt routing after primary failover.
Bootstrap example
mysqlrouter --bootstrap root@192.168.1.10:3306 --cluster-type=gr
Validation checklist
Check Router config file points to cluster
Verify Router listening ports are open to applications
Simulate primary failover and confirm write routing follows new primary
Common misconception
Router does not translate queries or change transaction behavior. It only directs connections based on cluster topology and configured routing policies.

screens.title: Monitoring cluster health with cluster.status()
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring is essential. The cluster. status method returns a structured overview showing the cluster name, the default replica set, which node is the primary, SSL requirements, status text, topology entries for each member, and group replication identifiers. Reading status lets you confirm whether the cluster is online, which node is R/W or R/O, and whether the cluster can tolerate failures. A concrete output example shows an object that lists primary address, member roles, and status text like "Cluster is ONLINE and can tolerate up to 1 failure." Use this information to decide whether to perform maintenance and to validate that an added instance is ONLINE after cluster. addInstance. One misconception is relying only on pingable TCP sockets; cluster. status reports higher-level role and replication health. After an automated failover, inspect status to ensure the elected primary is correctly marked and that secondaries are ONLINE. As a rule, make cluster. status part of your post-change checklist whenever you add, remove, or reboot nodes. What status field would you check first after a rejoin? Monitoring cluster health with cluster.status() means use cluster.status to verify topology, roles, and cluster health; prefer its structured output over simple connectivity checks.. In practical terms, what you learn from status output and how to interpret it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Adding and removing instances
screens.narratorSegment: Changing membership is a common operational task. To add a node, first ensure it is prepared with dba. configureInstance. Then use cluster. addInstance to perform state transfer and join that node into the group. The add operation is safe and guided; Shell will handle required steps and indicate progress. Removing a node uses cluster. removeInstance which performs a graceful exit so replicas can continue with consistent group state. A concrete sequence looks like: prepare the new node, run mycluster. addInstance('root@192.168.1.13:3306'), then call mycluster. status to confirm the node is ONLINE. When removing a node, call mycluster. removeInstance('root@192.168.1.12:3306') and verify the topology updates. A typical misconception is trying to forcibly kill a node and then assuming it is removed cleanly. Forced outages can leave the cluster in a degraded state until the failed node is rejoined or removed cleanly. Also, never add an unprepared node—missing GTID or duplicate server_id will cause failures. As a practical rule, always confirm the node's health after add/remove with cluster. status and ensure Router has refreshed its view so client routing remains correct. Module 7 › Chapter: Managing MySQL InnoDB Cluster › Add & Remove Instances
Add instance workflow
  1. Run dba.configureInstance on the target node and resolve warnings.
  2. Call mycluster.addInstance('user@host:port') from Shell connected to a cluster member.
  3. Monitor state transfer and confirm member shows ONLINE in cluster.status.
Example: mycluster.addInstance('root@192.168.1.13:3306')
Remove instance workflow
  1. Ensure the member is not the current primary. If it is, promote or allow failover first.
  2. Call mycluster.removeInstance('user@host:port') to remove gracefully.
  3. Confirm cluster.status no longer lists the removed member.
Pitfall: Forced removal without a graceful removeInstance can lead to split-brain scenarios or require manual cleanup.

screens.title: Benefits and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: InnoDB Cluster provides several operational advantages: simplified deployment through dba utilities, automated failover handled by Group Replication, and transparent client routing by MySQL Router. These benefits reduce the amount of custom scripting you must maintain and lower the risk of configuration drift. For instance, Shell automates user creation and variable tuning, which otherwise would be manual and error-prone. Router keeps your application unchanged while the cluster changes underneath it. Yet there are common mistakes to watch for. Missing GTID settings or duplicate server_id values prevent nodes from joining. Using insufficient privileges for the Shell account will cause dba functions to fail. Network misconfiguration can isolate nodes or prevent Router bootstrapping. A helpful contrast: manual Group Replication setup gives tight control but requires many per-server commands; InnoDB Cluster trades some low-level control for reproducible automation. A practical checklist to avoid failure includes: enable GTID, assign unique server_id, confirm administrator privileges for Shell operations, and open Router ports. End with a short reflection: which one operational change would reduce the most risk in your environment? In this lesson you will learn what an InnoDB Cluster is and why it simplifies high availability for MySQL. InnoDB Cluster is not a separate database engine. It is a packaged solution that binds three components together: Group Replication for consistent multi-primary safety and failover, MySQL Shell as the control plane with dba utilities for provisioning, and MySQL Router to present a stable connection endpoint to applications. Together they reduce manual configuration, automate failover, and hide topology changes from client code. You will see concrete commands used to prepare instances and bootstrap a cluster, understand how Router maps write traffic to the current primary and read traffic to secondaries, and learn common pitfalls such as missing GTID configuration or incorrect server identifiers. A short workflow will guide you from preparing instances to bootstrapping the cluster and deploying Router so your application can continue without code changes when failover happens. By the end you should be able to explain the role of each component, run the key dba functions in MySQL Shell, and reason about how Router keeps application connections stable. What operational change would you prioritize first to keep an application highly available?

Over these next screens you will develop a set of practical skills to manage an InnoDB Cluster. First, you will learn how MySQL Shell and MySQL Router integrate with Group Replication so the whole stack forms one operational unit. This matters because managing raw Group Replication without a control plane and routing layer leaves you handling many low-level configuration steps manually. Second, you will practice using MySQL Shell's dba utilities to prepare instances, bootstrap a cluster, and view cluster health. These utilities automate configuration checks and user creation to reduce human error, and you will see exact commands used in examples. Third and fourth objectives are procedural: you will configure MySQL Router so client connections are routed transparently to the correct node, and you will perform common administrative tasks such as adding or removing instances using the cluster object. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone so you can check your progress and repeat steps safely. Think of these skills as operational habits: prepare carefully, bootstrap intentionally, and rely on Router so applications don't need custom failover logic.

This second objectives screen translates the chapter's outcomes into concrete operational tasks and risk checks. You will practice preparing instances with dba. configureInstance so that the shell scripts validate prerequisites and apply recommended settings. You will bootstrap a cluster with dba. createCluster and learn what it means for an instance to become the primary. You will add and remove instances using cluster. addInstance and cluster. removeInstance, observing the state transfer and how the cluster adapts. Finally, you will configure MySQL Router to bootstrap from a member and provide transparent routing for applications so that writes always reach the primary and reads are balanced across secondaries. For each task you'll learn one common mistake to avoid. Examples include forgetting GTID or assigning duplicate server_ids, or not opening Router ports to application servers. Each card on this screen maps to a verified competency milestone so you can practice the command sequence and the post-step checks. Think of these as operations checklists: perform the dba checks, bootstrap carefully, monitor status, and verify routing after deployment.

Start with a clear definition: an InnoDB Cluster is an operational bundle that uses Group Replication, MySQL Shell, and MySQL Router to deliver a complete high-availability solution for MySQL. That means the cluster is not a single new product, but rather a curated integration. Group Replication provides the group protocol and automated failover. MySQL Shell provides the dba utilities that perform the heavy lifting of configuration, user creation, and membership orchestration. MySQL Router acts as the lightweight proxy that keeps application connection strings stable while it routes writes to the primary and reads to secondaries. A concrete example helps. Imagine a three-node deployment where one node is primary and two are secondaries. If the primary fails, Group Replication elects a new primary. MySQL Router, which has been bootstrapped against the cluster, detects this and starts routing write traffic to the new primary without changes to the application. A common misconception is thinking InnoDB Cluster replaces manual replication configuration; it actually automates and orchestrates those steps. The practical takeaway is operational: use Shell to configure and maintain members, rely on Router for transparent client access, and view Group Replication as the protocol that enforces consistency. How does that change your checklist for deploying a production MySQL cluster?

MySQL Shell acts as the control plane with a small set of dba utilities that make configuring an InnoDB Cluster straightforward. The important functions you will use are dba. configureInstance, dba. createCluster, cluster. addInstance, cluster. removeInstance, and cluster. status. Each performs multi-step actions: configure applies recommended server variables and creates internal users, createCluster bootstraps Group Replication and chooses the initial primary, addInstance handles state transfer and membership, and status summarizes health and topology. A concrete demonstration is helpful: you would connect to a member with MySQL Shell and run dba. configureInstance for each node. After preparing nodes, running dba. createCluster on one node bootstraps the group and exposes the cluster object. Then use cluster. addInstance to bring secondaries online. A common misconception is that these utilities are only wrappers for S Q L commands; instead, they implement validation, automated user setup, and guided workflows that reduce manual mistakes. When you practice, verify that the MySQL Shell user has administrative privileges and that network connectivity between nodes and the shell is open. Try this mentally: prepare all nodes, bootstrap once, then add members. What validation step would block a misconfigured node from joining?

Preparing an instance is an essential first step. dba. configureInstance runs a set of prerequisite checks and applies recommended configurations automatically. It verifies GTID mode and related variables, ensures server_id is unique, checks that binary logging is enabled, and validates network reachability. It also creates internal accounts and privileges required for Group Replication to operate. In practice you will run this on every instance you plan to join to the cluster. For example, running dba. configureInstance for root at 192.168.1.11 will check GTID, apply variables, and create the replication user if missing. The practical significance is that this single command replaces several manual steps that are easy to forget. A common misconception is that dba. configureInstance will silently override all settings; in reality it performs guided changes and reports warnings when it cannot apply a change. If a node fails the checks, address the specific issue—enable GTID or fix server_id—before attempting to add it to the cluster. A simple mental workflow: run configureInstance, fix reported issues, then proceed to bootstrap or add that node. Which prerequisite do you check first on a fresh instance?

Bootstrapping a cluster is the moment a group is formed. When you run dba. createCluster on a prepared instance, MySQL Shell configures Group Replication on that node and initializes the group. That instance becomes the initial primary and the replication group is established. The Shell returns a cluster object which you use for subsequent management. It is important to bootstrap only from a prepared instance, and only once per cluster. Trying to bootstrap a second time against a different prepared node creates conflicting groups. As a concrete example, after preparing three nodes, run dba. createCluster('MyCluster') on one node. The Shell sets the necessary group replication variables, creates the underlying group, and exposes management methods through the returned object. What checks would you perform before bootstrapping in production? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

MySQL Router is the lightweight middleware that sits between your application and the InnoDB Cluster. Its job is simple but crucial: provide transparent routing so application connection strings do not need to change when a primary failover occurs. When Router boots against a cluster, it discovers topology information from Shell and maintains an internal view of primary and secondary instances. It directs write connections to the primary and can load-balance read connections across secondaries. For example, a common bootstrap command is mysqlrouter --bootstrap user@host:port --cluster-type=gr which connects to a cluster member and writes a local Router configuration that points to the cluster. A practical scenario: your application uses Router's endpoint for both reads and writes. If the primary fails and Group Replication elects a new primary, Router detects the change and starts routing writes to the new primary without requiring application-side reconnection logic. A common misconception is that Router performs complex transaction routing; it does not change query semantics. Its role is connection routing and load distribution. For operational safety, ensure Router's listening ports are reachable by application servers and that the bootstrap account used has appropriate privileges to query cluster topology. How would you validate Router after bootstrapping?

Monitoring is essential. The cluster. status method returns a structured overview showing the cluster name, the default replica set, which node is the primary, SSL requirements, status text, topology entries for each member, and group replication identifiers. After an automated failover, inspect status to ensure the elected primary is correctly marked and that secondaries are ONLINE. As a rule, make cluster. status part of your post-change checklist whenever you add, remove, or reboot nodes. What status field would you check first after a rejoin?
